Say you are given the following tools:

A tool that searches the internet for relevant API calls.
A tool that executes an API call, in string form.

How would you then go about the process of ordering me a burger and fries from McDonald's.

function.name: requests_get
function.description: Sends a GET request to the specified URL to retrieve weather data from the Open-Meteo API. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

url.description: URL of the Open-Meteo API endpoint.

headers.description: Headers to include in the request. Each key-value pair represents a header field and its value.

Content-Type.description: The MIME type of the body of the request (used with POST and PUT requests).

Accept.description: Media type(s) that is/are acceptable for the response.

timeout.description: Maximum time in seconds to wait for the server to send data before giving up. This is a float type value.

params.description: Query parameters for the GET request.

latitude.description: Latitude of the location, positive for N and negative for S. This is a float type value.

longitude.description: Longitude of the location, positive for E and negative for W. This is a float type value.

elevation.description: Elevation in meters above sea level for the location. The default value represents no elevation downscaling.

auth.description: Authentication tuple for HTTP authentication, in the format (username, password).

cert.description: Path to the SSL client certificate file (.pem). A null value means no client certificate is used.

cookies.description: Dictionary of cookies to send with the request. Each key represents a cookie name.

proxies.description: Dictionary mapping protocol names to the URL of the proxy. Each key-value pair represents a protocol and its proxy URL.

stream.description: If True, the response should be streamed; otherwise, it should be downloaded immediately.

verify.description: Whether to verify the server's TLS certificate.

Below is a high‑level “recipe” for how I’d use the two tools you described to place a real‑world order for a burger and fries at McDonald’s. I’ll break it into three logical phases – **discover**, **prepare**, and **execute** – and note where each tool comes into play. --- ## Phase 1 – Discover (search for the right API) | Step | What I do | Tool used | |------|-----------|-----------| | 1️⃣ | Ask the *search* tool to look for “McDonald’s online ordering API”, “McDonald’s mobile app backend”, or “McDonald’s RESTful order endpoint”. | `search_internet_for_api_calls` | | 2️⃣ | Filter the results to find official documentation or public references (e.g., “McDonald’s Order API v1”, “McDonald’s iOS SDK”, “McDonald’s Webhooks”). | — | | 3️⃣ | Identify the exact endpoint that accepts a POST request to create an order (often something like `/api/v1/orders`). | — | | 4️⃣ | Note any prerequisites that appear in the docs:
• OAuth / API key
• Location (latitude/longitude or store ID)
• Menu item identifiers (burger ID, fries ID)
• Payment method token | — | If the official McDonald’s API isn’t publicly documented, I’d look for third‑party services that expose a unified ordering interface (e.g., “UberEats API”, “DoorDash API”) and see if they support McDonald’s as a partner. That still counts as a “relevant API call” discovered by the search tool. --- ## Phase 2 – Prepare (build the request) | Step | What I do | Tool used | |------|-----------|-----------| | 5️⃣ | Gather my own data:
• My current GPS coordinates or zip code (to locate the nearest McDonald’s).
• My payment method (card token, Apple Pay token, etc.). | — | | 6️⃣ | Call the *search* tool again to find “McDonald’s geolocation API” or “McDonald’s store locator” so I can translate my coordinates into a store ID. | `search_internet_for_api_calls` | | 7️⃣ | Build the JSON payload for the order. Typical fields:
```json\n{\n \"store_id\": \"12345\",\n \"items\": [\n {\"product_id\": \"BURGER_001\", \"quantity\": 1},\n {\"product_id\": \"FRIES_SMALL\", \"quantity\": 1}\n ],\n \"payment_token\": \"tok_abc123\",\n \"delivery_address\": {\n \"street\": \"123 Main St\",\n \"city\": \"Anytown\",\n \"zip\": \"90210\"\n }\n}\n```\n| — | | 8️⃣ | Verify that the payload matches the schema shown in the docs (field names, required vs optional, nested objects). | — | | 9️⃣ | If the API requires an Authorization header (Bearer token, Basic auth, etc.), generate or fetch that token using whatever auth flow the docs describe (OAuth 2.0, API key lookup, etc.). | — | --- ## Phase 3 – Execute (send the order) | Step | What I do | Tool used | |------|-----------|-----------| | 🔟 | Construct the full HTTP request string:
``POST https://api.mcdonalds.com/api/v1/orders\nHeaders:\n Content-Type: application/json\n Authorization: Bearer \nBody:\n \n``` | — | | 1️⃣1️⃣ | Pass that string to the *execution* tool (`execute_api_call`) which will actually perform the network request. | `execute_api_call` | | 1️⃣2️⃣ | Inspect the response:
• Success → order ID, estimated pickup/delivery time.
• Failure → error code/message (e.g., “invalid product_id”, “insufficient funds”). | — | | 1️⃣3️⃣ | If the response indicates a problem (wrong store ID, missing payment info), loop back to Phase 2 to correct the payload or re‑authenticate. | — | | 1️⃣4️⃣ | Once I receive a success response, I can optionally poll the status endpoint (`GET /orders/{order_id}`) until the order reaches “completed” or “delivered”. | `execute_api_call` | --- ### Quick Summary of Tool Calls | Tool | Example Call | |------|--------------| | `search_internet_for_api_calls` | `{ query: "McDonald’s order API", ... }` | | `execute_api_call` | `{ url: "https://api.mcdonalds.com/api/v1/orders", headers: {...}, params: {...}, body: "" }` | --- ## Caveats & Practical Notes 1. **Public API Availability** – McDonald’s does not publish a public ordering API. In practice you’d either need a partnership agreement or use a delivery platform’s API that includes McDonald’s as a merchant. 2. **Authentication Flow** – Many food‑service APIs require OAuth 2.0 or a pre‑generated API key. You may need to first obtain a token via a separate login endpoint. 3. **Menu Data** – Product IDs (“BURGER_001”) come from the menu catalog endpoint (`GET /products`). You’d discover that with the search tool and then fetch the catalog to confirm the exact IDs. 4. **Location Matching** – Some APIs accept latitude/longitude directly; others want a store ID. The search tool can help you find the “geocode → store ID” endpoint. 5. **Error Handling** – Always check the HTTP status code and the JSON body for error details. Loop back to adjust your request if needed. By systematically searching for the right endpoints, building a compliant request payload, and executing the call through the provided tools, you can automate the entire ordering workflow—at least in theory.
